claim: CD95 mediates leukocyte slow rolling upon binding of CD95-ligand (CD95L) that is presented by endothelial cells.
source: Here we show using an autoperfused flow chamber assay of whole blood neutrophils and intravital microscopy of the inflamed cremaster muscle that CD95 mediates leukocyte slow rolling, adhesion and transmigration upon binding of CD95-ligand (CD95L) that is presented by endothelial cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from autoperfused flow chamber assays and intravital microscopy experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: CD95 mediates leukocyte adhesion upon binding of CD95-ligand (CD95L) that is presented by endothelial cells.
source: Here we show using an autoperfused flow chamber assay of whole blood neutrophils and intravital microscopy of the inflamed cremaster muscle that CD95 mediates leukocyte slow rolling, adhesion and transmigration upon binding of CD95-ligand (CD95L) that is presented by endothelial cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from autoperfused flow chamber assays and intravital microscopy experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: CD95 mediates leukocyte transmigration upon binding of CD95-ligand (CD95L) that is presented by endothelial cells.
source: Here we show using an autoperfused flow chamber assay of whole blood neutrophils and intravital microscopy of the inflamed cremaster muscle that CD95 mediates leukocyte slow rolling, adhesion and transmigration upon binding of CD95-ligand (CD95L) that is presented by endothelial cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from autoperfused flow chamber assays and intravital microscopy experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: In myeloid cells, CD95 triggers activation of Syk-Btk/PLCγ2/Rap1 signaling that ultimately leads to integrin activation.
source: In myeloid cells, CD95 triggers activation of Syk-Btk/PLCγ2/Rap1 signaling that ultimately leads to integrin activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing phosphorylation of Syk, Btk, PLCγ2, and activation of Rap1 upon CD95L stimulation.

claim: CD95-deficient myeloid cells exhibit impaired bacterial clearance in an animal model of sepsis induced by cecal ligation and puncture (CLP).
source: Excitingly, CD95-deficient myeloid cells exhibit impaired bacterial clearance in an animal model of sepsis induced by cecal ligation and puncture (CLP).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing increased bacterial counts in CD95-deficient mice after CLP.

claim: Leukocyte recruitment comprises of a cascade with four major steps: slow rolling, firm adhesion, intraluminal crawling and trans-vessel migration.
source: Leukocyte recruitment comprises of a cascade with four major steps: slow rolling, firm adhesion, intraluminal crawling and trans-vessel migration (Ley et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ley et al., 2007.

claim: Slow rolling and firm adhesion are mediated by selectin- and chemokine-induced integrin signaling.
source: Slow rolling and firm adhesion are mediated by selectin- and chemokine-induced integrin signaling.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about leukocyte recruitment mechanisms.

claim: Selectin is expressed and presented to the vessel lumen by inflamed endothelial cells.
source: Selectin is expressed and presented to the vessel lumen by inflamed endothelial cells (Zarbock et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zarbock et al., 2011.

claim: E-selectin engagement with PSGL-1 and CD44 ligands induces activation of the Src family kinases (SFKs) Hck, Fgr and Lyn.
source: E-selectin engagement with PSGL-1 and CD44 ligands induces activation of the Src family kinases (SFKs) Hck, Fgr and Lyn (Yago et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yago et al., 2010.

claim: Activated Src family kinases phosphorylate and activate immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif (ITAM)-bearing adaptor protein Fc receptor common γ signaling chain (FcRγ) and DNAX activation protein of 12 kDa (DAP12).
source: which then phosphorylate and activate immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif (ITAM)-bearing adaptor protein Fc receptor common γ signaling chain (FcRγ) and DNAX activation protein of 12 kDa (DAP12) (Zarbock et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zarbock et al., 2008.

claim: Activated adaptor proteins recruit and phosphorylate spleen tyrosine kinase (Syk), which in turn activates Bruton's tyrosine kinase (Btk).
source: These activated adaptor proteins recruit and phosphorylate spleen tyrosine kinase (Syk), which in turn activates Bruton's tyrosine kinase (Btk) (Mueller et al., 2010; Yago et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mueller et al., 2010 and Yago et al., 2010.

claim: Btk activates the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), phospholipase C γ2 (PLCγ2) and p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (p38 MAPK) pathways that mediate the integrin signaling to induce slow rolling.
source: Btk further activates the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), phospholipase C γ2 (PLCγ2) and p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (p38 MAPK) pathways that mediate the integrin signaling to induce slow rolling.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about integrin signaling pathways.

claim: E-selectin- and integrin-mediated rolling crucially depend on Syk activation via binding to phosphorylated ITAM-domains.
source: E-selectin- and integrin-mediated rolling crucially depend on Syk activation via binding to phosphorylated ITAM-domains (Mueller et al., 2010; Yago et al., 2010; Zarbock et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mueller et al., 2010; Yago et al., 2010; and Zarbock et al., 2007.

claim: An ITAM-like motif was identified as a docking site for Src homology domain 2 (SH2)-containing proteins in CD95 of neutrophils.
source: Interestingly, an ITAM-like motif was identified as a docking site for Src homology domain 2 (SH2)-containing proteins in CD95 of neutrophils (Daigle et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Daigle et al., 2002.

claim: In CD95L-stimulated myeloid cells, Lyn is the major SFK that phosphorylates CD95's tyrosine, thereby allowing recruitment of Syk, which via the PI3K/MMP9 pathway results in myeloid cell migration to the inflammatory site.
source: In CD95L-stimulated myeloid cells, we identified Lyn as the major SFK that phosphorylates CD95's tyrosine, thereby allowing recruitment of Syk, which via the PI3K/MMP9 pathway results in myeloid cell migration to the inflammatory site (Letellier et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Letellier et al., 2010.

claim: CD95 (Fas/Apo-1) was initially described as a death receptor mediating apoptosis via formation of the death-inducing signal complex (DISC) which further leads to activation of downstream caspases and apoptosis.
source: CD95 (Fas/Apo-1) was initially described as a death receptor mediating apoptosis via formation of the death-inducing signal complex (DISC) which further leads to activation of downstream caspases and apoptosis (Peter et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Peter et al., 2007.

claim: In T cells the apoptotic cascade is prevented via formation of CD44-ezrin-actin-CD95 signaling complexes.
source: Interestingly, in T cells the apoptotic cascade is prevented via formation of CD44-ezrin-actin-CD95 signaling complexes (Mielgo et al., 2006, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mielgo et al., 2006, 2007.

claim: In B cells the CD95-FADD interaction is prevented by binding of Btk to CD95 via its kinase and Pleckstrin homology (PH) domain.
source: Likewise, in B cells the CD95-FADD interaction is prevented by binding of Btk to CD95 via its kinase and Pleckstrin homology (PH) domain (Uckun, 1998; Vassilev et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Uckun, 1998 and Vassilev et al., 1999.

claim: CD95 mediates slow rolling and adhesion of myeloid cells via activation of integrin through stimulation of Syk-Btk-PLCγ2 or Btk-PLCγ2 signaling pathways.
source: Here, we report that CD95 mediates slow rolling and adhesion of myeloid cells via activation of integrin through stimulation of Syk-Btk-PLCγ2 or Btk-PLCγ2 signaling pathways.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing phosphorylation of these signaling molecules and functional assays.

claim: CD95 in myeloid cells or CD95L in endothelial cells is required for myeloid cell recruitment in in vivo animal models of inflammation.
source: CD95 in myeloid cells or CD95L in endothelial cells is required for myeloid cell recruitment in in vivo animal models of inflammation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from intravital microscopy and peritonitis models.

claim: Deletion of CD95 in myeloid cells impairs bacterial clearance in systemic inflammation.
source: Further, deletion of CD95 in myeloid cells impairs bacterial clearance in systemic inflammation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CLP-induced sepsis model.

claim: Endothelial cell-derived CD95L serves as a chemokine in induction of neutrophil slow rolling and adhesion via integrin activation during inflammation.
source: Collectively, our data demonstrate that endothelial cell-derived CD95L serves as a chemokine in induction of neutrophil slow rolling and adhesion via integrin activation during inflammation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from flow chamber assays, intravital microscopy, and molecular signaling studies.

claim: 89 ± 2% of the rolling cells in the flow chamber have been identified as neutrophils in Lyz2<CreGFP> reporter mice.
source: In addition, using the Lyz2<CreGFP> reporter mice, 89 ± 2% of the rolling cells in the flow chamber have been identified as neutrophils (Chesnutt et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chesnutt et al., 2006.

claim: The rolling velocity of neutrophils is significantly reduced on E-selectin+ICAM1-coated chamber as compared to the E-selectin-coated chamber.
source: Consistent with previous reports, the rolling velocity of neutrophils is significantly reduced on E-selectin+ICAM1-coated chamber as compared to the E-selectin-coated chamber (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) (Jung and Ley, 1999; Chesnutt et al., 2006; Zarbock et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, and citations to Jung and Ley, 1999; Chesnutt et al., 2006; Zarbock et al., 2007.

claim: Intravenous injection of CD95L one hour prior to flow chamber assay significantly reduced the rolling velocity as compared to control counterparts.
source: Additional intravenous tail (i.v.) injection of CD95L one hour prior to flow chamber assay significantly reduced the rolling velocity as compared to control counterparts (Figure 1B,C; 1.55 ± 0.07 µm/s vs. 1.16 ± 0.03 µm/s).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C with specific velocity measurements.

claim: The rolling velocity of neutrophils in 50 μg/ml CD95L-coated chamber was significantly lower than in the control group.
source: The rolling velocity of neutrophils in 50 μg/ml CD95L-coated chamber was significantly lower than in the control group (Figure 1B,C; 1.55 ± 0.07 µm/s vs. 0.84 ± 0.09 µm/s).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C with specific velocity measurements.

claim: Flow chamber coated with 50 μg/ml CD95L showed the strongest effect on slow rolling as compared to other coating concentrations.
source: Flow chamber coated with 50 μg/ml CD95L showed the strongest effect on slow rolling as compared to other coating concentrations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CD95L-induced slow rolling was E-selectin-dependent.
source: Rolling cells in CD95L alone-coated or CD95L/ICAM1-coated chamber were not detectable which indicated that CD95L-induced slow rolling was E-selectin-dependent (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no rolling cells in the absence of E-selectin.

claim: CD95L i.v. injection or CD95L-coating increased the number of rolling cells in the flow chamber as compared to the control group.
source: In addition, CD95L i.v. injection or CD95L-coating increased the number of rolling cells in the flow chamber as compared to the control group (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CD95-deficient neutrophils rolled at a similar velocity as Fas<f/f> neutrophils.
source: Although CD95-deficient neutrophils rolled at a similar velocity as Fas<f/f>neutrophils (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), CD95L i.v.-injection or CD95L coating failed to reduce neutrophils' rolling velocity in Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Figure 1B.

claim: CD95L i.v.-injection or CD95L coating failed to reduce neutrophils' rolling velocity in Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice.
source: Although CD95-deficient neutrophils rolled at a similar velocity as Fas<f/f>neutrophils (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), CD95L i.v.-injection or CD95L coating failed to reduce neutrophils' rolling velocity in Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice showed significantly less rolling cells in CD95L-coated flow chamber or upon CD95L injection as compared to the WT mice under the same condition.
source: Interestingly, Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice showed significantly less rolling cells in CD95L-coated flow chamber or upon CD95L injection as compared to the WT mice under the same condition (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The effect of coated CD95L on neutrophil slow rolling was blocked by an integrin αL neutralizing antibody, anti-CD11a.
source: More importantly, the effect of coated CD95L on neutrophil slow rolling was blocked by an integrin αL neutralizing antibody, anti-CD11a, indicating that CD95L-induced slow rolling was integrin αL-dependent (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: CD95L-induced slow rolling was integrin αL-dependent.
source: More importantly, the effect of coated CD95L on neutrophil slow rolling was blocked by an integrin αL neutralizing antibody, anti-CD11a, indicating that CD95L-induced slow rolling was integrin αL-dependent (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the blocking experiment with anti-CD11a antibody shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Integrin αM neutralizing antibody, anti-CD11b, did not block CD95L-induced slow rolling.
source: However, integrin αM neutralizing antibody, anti-CD11b, did not block CD95L-induced slow rolling (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: >95% of all adherent and rolling leukocytes are neutrophils in the TNF-α-induced cremaster muscle inflammation model.
source: It has been reported that >95% of all adherent and rolling leukocytes are neutrophils in this model (Jung et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jung et al., 1998.

claim: The rolling velocity of leukocyte in Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice was not reduced in the TNF-α-induced cremaster muscle inflammation model.
source: Interestingly, the rolling velocity of leukocyte in Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice was not reduced (Figure 1G), indicating a redundant function of TNF-α and CD95 in modulation of rolling velocity, similar to the redundancy previously reported in a model of traumatic brain injury in mice (Bermpohl et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and a citation to Bermpohl et al., 2007.

claim: TNF was involved in neutrophil and T-cell adhesion via TNF-induced inside-out signaling.
source: Importantly, two studies showed that TNF was involved in neutrophil and T-cell adhesion via TNF-induced inside-out signaling (Lauterbach et al., 2008; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lauterbach et al., 2008 and Li et al., 2016.

claim: Naïve Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice expressed higher levels of TNFR2 but similar levels of TNFR1.
source: In order to clarify the redundant effect of TNF on CD95-deficiency, we stained neutrophils from blood of Fas<f/f> and Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice for TNF receptors (TNFR) and observed that naïve Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice expressed higher levels of TNFR2 but similar levels of TNFR1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from flow cytometry analysis of TNFR expression.

claim: At 6 hr after cecal ligation and puncture (CLP), neutrophils from Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice had higher expression of TNFR1 but similar expression of TNFR2.
source: However, at 6 hr after cecal ligation and puncture (CLP), neutrophils from Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice had higher expression of TNFR1 but similar expression of TNFR2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The numbers of adherent cells in Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice were reduced as compared to Fas<f/f> mice in the inflamed cremaster muscle.
source: Consistent with our previous report that CD95 triggers transmigration of myeloid cells to the inflammatory site (Letellier et al., 2010), the numbers of adherent cells and transmigrated cells in Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice were reduced as compared to Fas<f/f> mice (Figure 1H, and I),
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and a citation to Letellier et al., 2010.

claim: The numbers of transmigrated cells in Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice were reduced as compared to Fas<f/f> mice in the inflamed cremaster muscle.
source: Consistent with our previous report that CD95 triggers transmigration of myeloid cells to the inflammatory site (Letellier et al., 2010), the numbers of adherent cells and transmigrated cells in Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice were reduced as compared to Fas<f/f> mice (Figure 1H, and I),
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I and a citation to Letellier et al., 2010.

claim: Neutrophil slow rolling is mainly mediated by activation of lymphocyte function-associated antigen 1 (LFA-1, Integrin αLβ2).
source: Neutrophil slow rolling is mainly mediated by activation of lymphocyte function-associated antigen 1 (LFA-1, Integrin αLβ2) (Chesnutt et al., 2006; Zarbock et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chesnutt et al., 2006 and Zarbock et al., 2007.

claim: There was no difference in integrin αL and β2 expression between CD95-deficient neutrophils and Fas<f/f> neutrophils.
source: Similarly, in Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E), there was no difference in integrin αL and β2 expression between CD95-deficient neutrophils and Fas<f/f> neutrophils, but only an increase of integrin αM levels in CD95-deficient neutrophils (Figure 1—figure supplement 3F–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3F–I.

claim: There was an increase of integrin αM levels in CD95-deficient neutrophils.
source: Similarly, in Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E), there was no difference in integrin αL and β2 expression between CD95-deficient neutrophils and Fas<f/f> neutrophils, but only an increase of integrin αM levels in CD95-deficient neutrophils (Figure 1—figure supplement 3F–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3F–I.

claim: CD95-deficient neutrophils expressed the same level of CD44 as the Fas<f/f> neutrophils.
source: CD95-deficient neutrophils also expressed the same level of CD44, the ligand of E-seletin and P-selectin, as the Fas<f/f> neutrophils (Figure 1—figure supplement 3J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3J.

claim: The ratio of neutrophils and monocytes increased in the blood of Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice.
source: In addition, the ratio of neutrophils and monocytes increased in the blood of Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice, but T cells and B cells were not changed as compared to the control mice, and the absolute number of neutrophils in the blood of Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice was similar to the control counterparts (Figure 1—figure supplement 3K,L,M).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3K,L,M.

claim: The absolute number of neutrophils in the blood of Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice was similar to the control counterparts.
source: In addition, the ratio of neutrophils and monocytes increased in the blood of Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice, but T cells and B cells were not changed as compared to the control mice, and the absolute number of neutrophils in the blood of Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice was similar to the control counterparts (Figure 1—figure supplement 3K,L,M).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3K,L,M.

claim: CD95-induced slow rolling is not related to the up-regulation of cell surface expression level of integrins.
source: These results show that CD95-induced slow rolling is not related to the up-regulation of cell surface expression level of integrins.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no change in integrin surface expression upon CD95L stimulation or CD95 deletion.

claim: In inflamed tissue, inflammatory cytokines activate the expression of adhesion molecules, such as selectin and ICAM, and the synthesis of chemokines and lipid chemoattractants on the luminal surface of endothelial cells to facilitate the recruitment of leukocytes.
source: In inflamed tissue, inflammatory cytokines activate the expression of adhesion molecules, such as selectin and ICAM, and the synthesis of chemokines and lipid chemoattractants on the luminal surface of endothelial cells to facilitate the recruitment of leukocytes (Ley et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ley et al., 2007.

claim: The leukocyte rolling velocity was significantly increased in mice with CD95L deficiency in endothelial cells as compared to the Fasl<f/f> mice.
source: Interestingly, the leukocyte rolling velocity was significantly increased in mice with CD95L deficiency in endothelial cells as compared to the Fasl<f/f> mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The rolling flux fraction was reduced in Fasl<f/f>::Cdh5<CreERT2> mice.
source: Moreover, the rolling flux fraction which shows the percentage of rolling cells was reduced in Fasl<f/f>::Cdh5<CreERT2> mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Endothelial cell-derived CD95L is essential for leukocyte slow rolling during inflammation.
source: These observations indicate that endothelial cell-derived CD95L is essential for leukocyte slow rolling during inflammation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing increased rolling velocity and reduced rolling flux fraction in endothelial CD95L-deficient mice.

claim: The numbers of adherent cells in the inflamed venules were reduced in Fasl<f/f>::Cdh5<CreERT2> mice as compared to the control litter mates.
source: In line with the results from Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice, the numbers of adherent cells in the inflamed venules and transmigrated cells in the cremaster muscle were also reduced in Fasl<f/f>::Cdh5<CreERT2> mice as compared to the control litter mates (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E, F.

claim: The numbers of transmigrated cells in the cremaster muscle were reduced in Fasl<f/f>::Cdh5<CreERT2> mice as compared to the control litter mates.
source: In line with the results from Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice, the numbers of adherent cells in the inflamed venules and transmigrated cells in the cremaster muscle were also reduced in Fasl<f/f>::Cdh5<CreERT2> mice as compared to the control litter mates (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E, F.

claim: The number of peritoneal neutrophils at 6 hr after thioglycollate injection was significantly reduced in endothelial-CD95L deficient mice as compared to control counterparts.
source: The number of peritoneal neutrophils at 6 hr after thioglycollate injection was significantly reduced in endothelial-CD95L deficient mice as compared to control counterparts (Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Deletion of CD95 in the endothelial compartment (Fas<f/f>::Cdh5<CreERT2>) did not affect thioglycolate-induced neutrophil recruitment to the inflamed peritoneum.
source: Nonetheless, deletion of CD95 in the endothelial compartment (Fas<f/f>::Cdh5<CreERT2>) did not affect thioglycolate-induced neutrophil recruitment to the inflamed peritoneum (Figure 2J, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The cell surface expression of adhesion molecules, E-selectin, ICAM1 and ICAM2 was similar in CD95L-deleted and non-deleted endothelial cells, with the exception of cell surface expression of P-selectin that was reduced.
source: Notably, the cell surface expression of adhesion molecules, E-selectin, ICAM1 and ICAM2 was similar in CD95L-deleted and non-deleted endothelial cells, with the exception of cell surface expression of P-selectin that was reduced (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–G.

claim: Deletion of CD95 in myeloid cells had no impact on ICAM1 and selectin levels in endothelial cells.
source: Similarly, deletion of CD95 in myeloid cells had no impact on ICAM1 and selectin levels in endothelial cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H–J.

claim: The ratio of different leukocyte populations in the blood was not significantly changed in Fasl<f/f>::Cdh5<CreERT2> mice before or after tamoxifen induction as compared to the control mice.
source: Additionally, the ratio of different leukocyte populations in the blood and the absolute number of blood neutrophils were not significantly changed in Fasl<f/f>::Cdh5<CreERT2> mice before or after tamoxifen induction as compared to the control mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B,C.

claim: The absolute number of blood neutrophils was not significantly changed in Fasl<f/f>::Cdh5<CreERT2> mice before or after tamoxifen induction as compared to the control mice.
source: Additionally, the ratio of different leukocyte populations in the blood and the absolute number of blood neutrophils were not significantly changed in Fasl<f/f>::Cdh5<CreERT2> mice before or after tamoxifen induction as compared to the control mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B,C.

claim: The involvement of endothelial cell-derived CD95L in leukocyte slow rolling and transmigration is not related to the change of adhesion molecule expression level on the luminal surface of blood vessels or the homeostasis of leukocytes in the blood stream.
source: These data demonstrate that the involvement of endothelial cell-derived CD95L in leukocyte slow rolling and transmigration is not related to the change of adhesion molecule expression level on the luminal surface of blood vessels or the homeostasis of leukocytes in the blood stream.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no significant changes in adhesion molecule expression or leukocyte populations.

claim: E-selectin engagement triggers a signaling cascade which cooperates with chemokine signals to facilitate neutrophil rolling and adhesion during inflammation.
source: E-selectin engagement triggers a signaling cascade which cooperates with chemokine signals to facilitate neutrophil rolling and adhesion during inflammation (Zarbock et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zarbock et al., 2007.

claim: E-selectin is expressed by inflamed endothelial cells and engages PSGL-1, CD44 and other ligands in neutrophils.
source: E-selectin is expressed by inflamed endothelial cells and engages PSGL-1, CD44 and other ligands in neutrophils (Xia et al., 2002; Katayama et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Xia et al., 2002 and Katayama et al., 2005.

claim: E-selectin activates SFKs which in turn initiate a signaling pathway involving the activation of ITAM bearing adaptors, Syk, Btk, PLCγ2, P38 and PI3Kγ.
source: Upon ligand engagement, it has been reported that E-selectin activates SFKs which in turn initiate a signaling pathway involving the activation of ITAM bearing adaptors, Syk, Btk, PLCγ2, P38 and PI3Kγ (Yago et al., 2010; Mueller et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yago et al., 2010 and Mueller et al., 2010.

claim: CD95L triggers the recruitment of myeloid cells to inflammatory sites via SFK-Syk-PI3K pathway.
source: We have previously shown that CD95L triggers the recruitment of myeloid cells to inflammatory sites via SFK-Syk-PI3K pathway (Letellier et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Letellier et al., 2010.

claim: Activation of CD95 increased phosphorylation of Syk, Btk and PLCγ2.
source: Activation of CD95 increased phosphorylation of Syk, Btk and PLCγ2 (Figure 3A and quantified analysis in Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, B, C.

claim: CD95-mediated phosphorylation of PLCγ2 greatly decreased in macrophages isolated from Syk-/- mice as compared to wild type (WT) cells.
source: CD95-mediated phosphorylation of PLCγ2 greatly decreased in macrophages isolated from Syk-/- mice as compared to wild type (WT) cells (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, C.

claim: The reduced basal level of p-PLCγ2 in Syk-/- cells indicates that Syk is not only involved in CD95L-mediated phosphorylation of PLCγ2 but also acts as a hub for other ligands.
source: The reduced basal level of p-PLCγ2 in Syk-/- cells indicates that Syk is not only involved in CD95L-mediated phosphorylation of PLCγ2 but also acts as a hub for other ligands.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of reduced basal p-PLCγ2 levels in Syk-/- cells.

claim: The upregulated phosphorylation of Btk was still present in Syk-/- as compared to WT cells.
source: However, the upregulated phosphorylation of Btk was still present in Syk-/- as compared to WT cells (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, B.

claim: Binding of CD95 to Btk was detected following CD95L stimulation.
source: To examine this interaction we pulled down Btk from the lysates of CD95L-treated macrophages by immunoprecipitation. Binding of CD95 to Btk was detected following CD95L stimulation (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: PCI-32765 fully blocked the basal and CD95-induced phosphorylation of Btk and PLCγ2.
source: PCI-32765 fully blocked the basal and CD95-induced phosphorylation of Btk and PLCγ2 (Figure 3E,F,G), but not the phosphorylation of Syk (Figure 3H), which indicates that the phosphorylation of PLCγ2 is Btk-dependent and that Btk is an essential mediator for CD95-induced PLCγ2 activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E, F, G, H.

claim: PCI-32765 did not block the phosphorylation of Syk.
source: PCI-32765 fully blocked the basal and CD95-induced phosphorylation of Btk and PLCγ2 (Figure 3E,F,G), but not the phosphorylation of Syk (Figure 3H), which indicates that the phosphorylation of PLCγ2 is Btk-dependent and that Btk is an essential mediator for CD95-induced PLCγ2 activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The phosphorylation of PLCγ2 is Btk-dependent.
source: PCI-32765 fully blocked the basal and CD95-induced phosphorylation of Btk and PLCγ2 (Figure 3E,F,G), but not the phosphorylation of Syk (Figure 3H), which indicates that the phosphorylation of PLCγ2 is Btk-dependent and that Btk is an essential mediator for CD95-induced PLCγ2 activation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the Btk inhibitor experiment showing blocked PLCγ2 phosphorylation.

claim: Btk is an essential mediator for CD95-induced PLCγ2 activation.
source: PCI-32765 fully blocked the basal and CD95-induced phosphorylation of Btk and PLCγ2 (Figure 3E,F,G), but not the phosphorylation of Syk (Figure 3H), which indicates that the phosphorylation of PLCγ2 is Btk-dependent and that Btk is an essential mediator for CD95-induced PLCγ2 activation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the Btk inhibitor experiment showing blocked PLCγ2 phosphorylation.

claim: There are two signaling branches downstream of CD95: CD95/SFK/Syk/Btk/PLCγ2 and CD95/SFK/Btk/PLCγ2.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate the presence of two signaling branches downstream of CD95: CD95/SFK/Syk/Btk/PLCγ2 and CD95/SFK/Btk/PLCγ2 (Figure 3I).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing Btk phosphorylation in Syk-/- cells and the requirement of Btk for PLCγ2 phosphorylation.

claim: Immobilized CD95L-induced slow rolling was abolished in PCI-32765 pretreated mice in the autoperfused flow chamber assay.

evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: CD95L-induced slow rolling was Btk-dependent.
source: More importantly, immobilized CD95L-induced slow rolling was abolished in PCI-32765 pretreated mice in the autoperfused flow chamber assay, implying that CD95L-induced slow rolling was Btk-dependent (Figure 3J).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the Btk inhibitor experiment showing abolished slow rolling.

claim: The common final step for integrin activation has been revealed as binding of talin1 and kindlin-3 to the cytoplasmic domain of β integrin which in turn breaks the salt bridges between the cytosolic domains of integrin α and β subunits and induces integrin conformational changes.

claim: Recruitment of talin1 to LFA-1 is Rap1a-dependent.
source: Recruitment of talin1 to LFA-1 is Rap1a-dependent (Lefort et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lefort et al., 2012.

claim: Significant activation of Rap1 was observed in neutrophils 15 min after CD95L stimulation.

evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A, B.

claim: CD95L-treated and control neutrophils exhibited similar levels of integrin αL, integrin αM and integrin β2 expression.
source: Of note, CD95L-treated and control neutrophils exhibited similar levels of integrin αL, integrin αM and integrin β2 expression (Figure 4—figure supplement A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement A–D.

claim: KIM127 recognizes an epitope of β2 subunit of human LFA-1 when it is extended.
source: KIM127 recognizes an epitope of β2 subunit of human LFA-1 when it is extended (Beglova et al., 2002)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Beglova et al., 2002.

claim: mab24 binds to the epitope of I-like domain in β2 subunit of human LFA-1 only if this is accessible as in the high-affinity state.
source: whereas mab24 binds to the epitope of I-like domain in β2 subunit of human LFA-1 only if this is accessible as in the high-affinity state (Lu et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lu et al., 2001.

claim: Significantly increased binding of KIM127 and mab24 was observed in cells treated with soluble CD95L.
source: We observed significantly increased binding of KIM127 and mab24 in cells treated with soluble CD95L (Figure 4C,D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C, D, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: In the absence of coated E-selectin, soluble CD95L showed no effect on KIM127 and mab24 binding.
source: Notably, in the absence of coated E-selectin, soluble CD95L showed no effect on KIM127 and mab24 binding (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–G.

claim: CD95L treatment induces integrin conformational changes including its extension and full activation in an E-selectin-dependent manner.
source: These data indicate that CD95L treatment induces integrin conformational changes including its extension and full activation in an E-selectin-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the reporter antibody binding experiments showing increased KIM127 and mab24 binding in an E-selectin-dependent manner.

claim: CD95L-activated neutrophils showed significant binding of soluble ICAM1 as compared to the non-treated group.
source: CD95L-activated neutrophils showed significant binding of soluble ICAM1 as compared to the non-treated group (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CD95 signaling induces integrin activation.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that CD95 signaling induces integrin activation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing integrin conformational changes and increased ICAM1 binding upon CD95L stimulation.

claim: A signalosome consisting of Src family kinase Hck, Btk, WASp and PLCγ2 has been identified to be indispensable for fMLF-induced MAC-1 activation required for neutrophil recruitment.
source: Specifically, a signalosome consisting of Src family kinase Hck, Btk, WASp and PLCγ2 has been identified to be indispensable for fMLF-induced MAC-1 activation required for neutrophil recruitment (Volmering et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Volmering et al., 2016.

claim: Binding of CD95 to integrin αL was detected by PLA in dHL60 cells.
source: Indeed, binding of CD95 to integrin αL was detected by PLA in dHL60 cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: CD95L treatment significantly enhanced the binding of CD95 to integrin αL, as shown by increased number of PLA signal of CD95-integrin clusters.
source: CD95L treatment significantly enhanced this binding, as shown by increased number of PLA signal of CD95-integrin clusters (Figure 4G) and a ratio of PLA signal positive cells (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G, H.

claim: Among the PLA positive cells, CD95L treatment increased the number and integrated density of PLA signal as compared to the non-treated control.
source: Among the PLA positive cells, CD95L treatment increased the number and integrated density of PLA signal as compared to the non-treated control (Figure 4I,J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I, J.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of integrin αL from lysates of CD95L-treated mouse macrophages revealed a stimulation-dependent association of CD95 with integrin αL.
source: Moreover, immunoprecipitation of integrin αL from lysates of CD95L-treated mouse macrophages, revealed a stimulation-dependent association of CD95 with integrin αL (Figure 4K).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: Integrin αM did not bind to CD95 upon CD95L stimulation.
source: However, integrin αM did not bind to CD95 upon CD95L stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Activation of CD95 leads to the assembly of multiprotein complexes including integrins.
source: Collectively, our data indicate that activation of CD95 leads to the assembly of multiprotein complexes including integrins and that CD95 mediates integrin activation required for rolling and adhesion of myeloid cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the PLA and co-immunoprecipitation data showing CD95-integrin association.

claim: CD95 mediates integrin activation required for rolling and adhesion of myeloid cells.
source: Collectively, our data indicate that activation of CD95 leads to the assembly of multiprotein complexes including integrins and that CD95 mediates integrin activation required for rolling and adhesion of myeloid cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data showing CD95-integrin association, integrin activation, and functional effects on rolling and adhesion.

claim: Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice demonstrated significantly higher CFU in peritoneal lavage liquid as compared to the Fas<f/f> littermate control mice at 6 hr after CLP.

claim: Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice demonstrated significantly higher CFU in blood as compared to the Fas<f/f> littermate control mice at 6 hr after CLP.
source: Importantly, Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice demonstrated significantly higher CFU in peritoneal lavage liquid and blood as compared to the Fas<f/f> littermate control mice (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: CFU in spleen homogenate was elevated in Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice, but was not significantly higher.
source: CFU in spleen homogenate was also elevated, but was not significantly higher (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Peritoneal neutrophil infiltration in Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice was reduced as compared to the Fas<f/f> littermate control mice.
source: Moreover, peritoneal neutrophil infiltration in Fas<f/f>::Lyz2<Cre> mice was reduced as compared to the Fas<f/f> littermate control mice (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: CD95 in myeloid cells is involved in mounting an effective bacterial clearance response during systemic inflammation via recruiting neutrophils to the inflammatory sites.
source: These data indicate that CD95 in myeloid cells is involved in mounting an effective bacterial clearance response during systemic inflammation via recruiting neutrophils to the inflammatory sites.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing increased bacterial load and reduced neutrophil infiltration in CD95-deficient mice.

claim: Inflammation induces CD95L expression in endothelial cells.
source: In summary, inflammation induces CD95L expression in endothelial cells (Sata and Walsh, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sata and Walsh, 1998.

claim: CD95 together with E-selectin orchestrate signaling events leading to integrin activation that finally result in slow rolling and adhesion of myeloid cells.
source: CD95 together with E-selectin orchestrate signaling events leading to integrin activation that finally result in slow rolling and adhesion of myeloid cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined experimental data showing E-selectin-dependent CD95L-induced integrin activation and slow rolling.

claim: CD95-induced leukocyte infiltration was first found in early studies aiming at inducing apoptosis of tumor cells in vivo.
source: CD95-induced leukocyte infiltration was first found in early studies aiming at inducing apoptosis of tumor cells in vivo (Arai et al., 1997; Seino et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Arai et al., 1997 and Seino et al., 1997.

claim: Transplantation of CD95L-overexpressing/CD95-negative tumor cells induced a dramatic neutrophil infiltration into the tumor xenografts.
source: In these studies, transplantation of CD95L-overexpressing/CD95-negative tumor cells induced a dramatic neutrophil infiltration into the tumor xenografts.
evidence: The claim is based on established findings from previous studies.

claim: Soluble CD95L induces the transmigration of human neutrophils in vitro in Boyden chamber assays.
source: Other studies using Boyden chamber assays demonstrated that soluble CD95L induces the transmigration of human neutrophils in vitro (Seino et al., 1998; Ottonello et al., 1999; Dupont and Warrens, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Seino et al., 1998; Ottonello et al., 1999; and Dupont and Warrens, 2007.

claim: CD95 is involved in induction of slow rolling and adhesion of neutrophils.
source: The present study shows that CD95 is involved in induction of slow rolling and adhesion of neutrophils, and that these steps are blocked in CD95-deficient neutrophils, indicating that CD95 induces slow rolling via a direct effect on neutrophils and not via induction of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the present study.

claim: CD95 induces slow rolling via a direct effect on neutrophils and not via induction of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines.
source: The present study shows that CD95 is involved in induction of slow rolling and adhesion of neutrophils, and that these steps are blocked in CD95-deficient neutrophils, indicating that CD95 induces slow rolling via a direct effect on neutrophils and not via induction of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing direct effects in CD95-deficient neutrophils.

claim: Coating of the flow chamber with CD95L alone was not sufficient to induce leukocyte tethering (capturing).
source: However, coating of the flow chamber with CD95L alone was not sufficient to induce leukocyte tethering (capturing), indicating that E-selectin is required for CD95-mediated slow rolling.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from flow chamber assays.

claim: E-selectin is required for CD95-mediated slow rolling.
source: However, coating of the flow chamber with CD95L alone was not sufficient to induce leukocyte tethering (capturing), indicating that E-selectin is required for CD95-mediated slow rolling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no tethering with CD95L alone.

claim: Selectin ligands PSGL-1 and CD44 are enriched in lipid rafts.
source: It has been shown that selectin ligands PSGL-1 and CD44 are enriched in lipid rafts (Miner et al., 2008; Neame et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Miner et al., 2008 and Neame et al., 1995.

claim: The three SFKs of neutrophils, Fgr, Hck, Lyn, associate with cholesterol-dependent membrane rafts.
source: In addition, the three SFKs of neutrophils, Fgr, Hck, Lyn, which are activated upon the engagement of selectin to its ligands (Yago et al., 2010), also associate with cholesterol-dependent membrane rafts (Lowell, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yago et al., 2010 and Lowell, 2004.

claim: Neutrophil slow rolling has been reported to be dependent on intact lipid microdomains to signal slow rolling on E-selectin and P-selectin.
source: Interestingly, neutrophil slow rolling has been reported to be dependent on intact lipid microdomains to signal slow rolling on E-selectin and P-selectin (Yago et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yago et al., 2010.

claim: The clustering of lipid microdomains is regulated by the actin cytoskeleton.
source: The clustering of lipid microdomains is regulated by the actin cytoskeleton (Chichili and Rodgers, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chichili and Rodgers, 2007.

claim: Ezrin/radixin/moesin (ERM) proteins associate with PSGL-1 and CD44 through their cytoplasmic domains.
source: Ezrin/radixin/moesin (ERM) proteins, which link the cytoskeleton to integral membrane proteins via their FERM domains, associate with PSGL-1 and CD44 through their cytoplasmic domains (Yonemura et al., 1998; Urzainqui et al., 2002).

claim: Ligation of PSGL-1 to selectin recruits Syk to an atypical ITAM on ERM proteins bound to the cytoplasmic domain of PSGL-1.
source: Moreover, ligation of PSGL-1 to selectin recruits Syk to an atypical ITAM on ERM proteins bound to the cytoplasmic domain of PSGL-1 (Urzainqui et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Urzainqui et al., 2002.

claim: Leukocyte rolling requires the formation of multiprotein complexes at the plasma membrane.
source: Thus, leukocyte rolling requires the formation of multiprotein complexes at the plasma membrane.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the described interactions between selectin ligands, ERM proteins, and signaling molecules.

claim: CD95 clustering is accompanied by reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton and aggregation of lipid microdomains.
source: CD95 clustering is accompanied by reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton and aggregation of lipid microdomains (Söderström et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Söderström et al., 2005.

claim: CD95 clustering in sphingolipid-rich membrane microdomains is necessary for the induction of CD95 signaling.
source: Accordingly, CD95 clustering in sphingolipid-rich membrane microdomains is necessary for the induction of CD95 signaling (Grassme et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Grassme et al., 2001.

claim: CD95 indirectly associates with actin via direct and specific binding to ezrin FERM domains.
source: CD95 indirectly associates with actin via direct and specific binding to ezrin FERM domains (Lozupone et al., 2004), and the organization of the microfilaments affects the outcome of CD95 stimulation (Parlato et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lozupone et al., 2004 and Parlato et al., 2000.

claim: The organization of the microfilaments affects the outcome of CD95 stimulation.
source: CD95 indirectly associates with actin via direct and specific binding to ezrin FERM domains (Lozupone et al., 2004), and the organization of the microfilaments affects the outcome of CD95 stimulation (Parlato et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Parlato et al., 2000.

claim: CD44 has been reported to bind to CD95 via ezrin to block the apoptotic signal transduction.
source: In addition, CD44 has been reported to bind to CD95 via ezrin to block the apoptotic signal transduction (Mielgo et al., 2006, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mielgo et al., 2006, 2007.

claim: CD95 may be a part of a multiprotein complex encompassing selectin ligands, SFKs and cytoskeletal proteins that orchestrate leukocyte rolling.
source: These findings suggest that CD95 may also be a part of a multiprotein complex encompassing selectin ligands, SFKs and cytoskeletal proteins that orchestrate leukocyte rolling.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the described interactions and properties of CD95.

claim: Ligand binding to external domains causes conformational changes that increase ligand affinity, and formation of integrin clustering, which in turn results in SFK autophosphorylation and Syk kinase activation in the outside-in integrin pathway.
source: Ligand binding to external domains causes conformational changes that increase ligand affinity, and formation of integrin clustering, which in turn results in SFK autophosphorylation and Syk kinase activation in the outside-in integrin pathway (Abram and Lowell, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Abram and Lowell, 2009.

claim: SFK and Syk kinases can directly interact with the cytoplasmic domain of β2, and β3 integrins.
source: SFK and Syk kinases can directly interact with the cytoplasmic domain of β2, and β3 integrins (Arias-Salgado et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Arias-Salgado et al., 2003.

claim: ITAM containing adaptor proteins DAP12 and FcRγ couples Syk to integrins.
source: In addition, ITAM containing adaptor proteins DAP12 and FcRγ couples Syk to integrins (Mócsai et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mócsai et al., 2006.

claim: The ITAM-like YXXL motif of CD95 is involved in the CD95-Lyn-Syk signaling cascade leading to myeloid cell transmigration.
source: The ITAM-like YXXL motif of CD95 is involved in the CD95-Lyn-Syk signaling cascade leading to myeloid cell transmigration (Letellier et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Letellier et al., 2010.

claim: CD95 might indirectly impact myeloid cell recruitment by promoting secretion of inflammatory cytokines.
source: Alternatively, CD95 might indirectly impact myeloid cell recruitment by promoting secretion of inflammatory cytokines, as already reported in a variety of cell types (Altemeier et al., 2007; Dupont and Warrens, 2007; Park et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2010a).

claim: CD95 in apoptotic cells induced the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, which in turn attracted myeloid cells.

claim: The upregulation of selectins and ICAMs in endothelial cells and selectin- and ICAM-ligands in leukocytes play important roles in rolling and adhesion.
source: The upregulation of selectins and ICAMs in endothelial cells and selectin- and ICAM-ligands in leukocytes play important roles in rolling and adhesion (Pober and Sessa, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pober and Sessa, 2007.

claim: CD95L stimulation or CD95/CD95L deletion in endothelial cells have no impact on the expression level of adhesion molecules in endothelial cells.
source: Unlike the effect of TNF-α on endothelial cells, CD95L stimulation or CD95/CD95L deletion in endothelial cells have no impact on the expression level of adhesion molecules in endothelial cells.

claim: Crosslinking of CD95 with antibody rapidly triggers down-modulation of L-selectin, CD44, LFAα and LFAβ in CD95-sensitive T cell blasts.
source: A previous study has reported that crosslinking of CD95 with antibody rapidly triggers down-modulation of L-selectin, CD44, LFAα and LFAβ in CD95-sensitive T cell blasts (Kabelitz et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kabelitz et al., 1996.

claim: In vitro or in vivo treatment with CD95L, or CD95 deletion in myeloid cells did not change cell surface expression levels of most integrins.
source: In our study, in vitro or in vivo treatment with CD95L, or CD95 deletion in myeloid cells did not change cell surface expression levels of most integrins, which shows a cell type dependent effect of CD95 on the expression of adhesion molecules.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the present study.

claim: CD95-induced neutrophil slow rolling is independent of regulation of adhesion molecules.
source: These results demonstrate that CD95-induced neutrophil slow rolling is independent of regulation of adhesion molecules.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no change in adhesion molecule expression.

claim: Endothelial cells play a pivotal role in leukocyte recruitment by synthesizing and presenting chemokines and leukocyte adhesion molecules during inflammation.
source: Endothelial cells play a pivotal role in leukocyte recruitment by synthesizing and presenting chemokines and leukocyte adhesion molecules during inflammation (Pober and Sessa, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pober and Sessa, 2007.

claim: CD95L has been shown to be expressed by endothelial cells.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sata and Walsh, 1998.

claim: Overexpression of CD95L by adenovirus transduction in endothelial cells markedly attenuated TNF-α-induced T cell and macrophage infiltration, and adherent mononuclear cells underwent apoptosis.
source: Overexpression of CD95L by adenovirus transduction in endothelial cells markedly attenuated TNF-α-induced T cell and macrophage infiltration, and adherent mononuclear cells underwent apoptosis (Sata and Walsh, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sata and Walsh, 1998.

claim: Tumor endothelial cells selectively and highly express CD95L, which serves as a barrier to prevent the infiltration of CD8 cells via induction of apoptosis in the establishment of immune tolerance.
source: Along this line, tumor endothelial cells selectively and highly express CD95L, which serves as a barrier to prevent the infiltration of CD8 cells via induction of apoptosis in the establishment of immune tolerance (Motz et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Motz et al., 2014.

claim: Deletion of CD95L in endothelial cells impairs neutrophil recruitment in inflamed cremaster muscle and thioglycolate-induced peritonitis.
source: Contrary to the apoptotic effect of endothelial cell-derived CD95L, the present study shows that deletion of CD95L in endothelial cells impairs neutrophil recruitment in inflamed cremaster muscle and thioglycolate-induced peritonitis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the present study.

claim: Endothelial cell-derived CD95L may serve as a chemokine to induce myeloid cell recruitment during inflammation.
source: Together, these data indicate that endothelial cell-derived CD95L may serve as a chemokine to induce myeloid cell recruitment during inflammation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing impaired neutrophil recruitment in endothelial CD95L-deficient mice.

claim: Endothelial cells basally express CD95L.
source: Endothelial cells are known to basally express CD95L (Sata and Walsh, 1998), however, as shown by our study on CD95L-induced slow rolling in the autoperfused flow chamber assay, CD95L might only induce slow rolling in an inflammatory setting, as this function requires additional presentation of E-selectin by endothelial cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sata and Walsh, 1998.

claim: CD95L might only induce slow rolling in an inflammatory setting, as this function requires additional presentation of E-selectin by endothelial cells.
source: Endothelial cells are known to basally express CD95L (Sata and Walsh, 1998), however, as shown by our study on CD95L-induced slow rolling in the autoperfused flow chamber assay, CD95L might only induce slow rolling in an inflammatory setting, as this function requires additional presentation of E-selectin by endothelial cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing E-selectin-dependence of CD95L-induced slow rolling.

claim: Inflammatory cytokines might increase CD95L levels in endothelial cells.

claim: IFNγ activates CD95L promoter activity in T-cells.
source: Along this line, IFNγ activates CD95L promoter activity in T-cells (Kirchhoff et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kirchhoff et al., 2002.

claim: Integrin signaling plays important roles in regulating cancer 'stemness', metastasis and drug resistance.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Seguin et al., 2015.

claim: CD95 is now recognized as an inducer of tumor cell growth and invasion.
source: As CD95 is now recognized as an inducer of tumor cell growth and invasion (Martin-Villalba et al., 2013; Peter et al., 2015), it is of great importance to study the CD95-induced integrin signaling in tumor progression.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Martin-Villalba et al., 2013 and Peter et al., 2015.

claim: Tumor growth and metastasis are promoted by myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC).
source: On the other hand, tumor growth and metastasis are promoted by myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC) (Condamine et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Condamine et al., 2015.

claim: Blockade of endothelial cells-derived CD95L in order to inhibit MDSCs recruitment to tumor might be used as a potential strategy for cancer therapy.
source: Blockade of endothelial cells-derived CD95L in order to inhibit MDSCs recruitment to tumor might be used as a potential strategy for cancer therapy.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the findings about CD95L's role in myeloid cell recruitment.

claim: Effective removal of infectious organisms is of utmost importance to attenuate the early onset of sepsis.
source: Effective removal of infectious organisms is of utmost importance to attenuate the early onset of sepsis (Bosmann and Ward, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bosmann and Ward, 2013.

claim: Mice with a global impairment of CD95 activity, Faslpr/lpr and Fasgld/gld mice, develop severe diarrhoea and showed impaired bacterial clearance in a bacterial-induced gut infection model.
source: It has been reported that mice with a global impairment of CD95 activity, Faslpr/lpr and Fasgld/gld mice, develop severe diarrhoea and showed impaired bacterial clearance in a bacterial-induced gut infection model (Pearson et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pearson et al., 2013.

claim: Myeloid cells require CD95 activity to efficiently infiltrate into the inflammatory sites and clear bacteria following CLP-induced sepsis.
source: We now show that myeloid cells require CD95 activity to efficiently to infiltrate into the inflammatory sites and clear bacteria following CLP-induced sepsis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the CLP-induced sepsis model.

claim: Therapies aimed at interfering with CD95's activity can be used for the treatment of diseases with a major cell-extravasation component such as cancer progression and inflammation.
source: Altogether, this study shows a chemoattractant effect of endothelial cell-derived CD95L in induction of neutrophil slow rolling and adhesion via integrin activation. Both cancer cells and immune cells exhibit very high levels of CD95 surface expression. Therapies aimed at interfering with CD95's activity can be used for the treatment of diseases with a major cell-extravasation component such as cancer progression and inflammation.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the findings about CD95's role in cell recruitment and its expression in cancer and immune cells.
